name: __reverse_impl(_BidirectionalIterator, _BidirectionalIterator, bidirectional_iterator_tag)
prose: Template function in libc++ (__cxx03/__algorithm/reverse.h) taking its two iterators by value. Loop: while __first != __last, it decrements __last; if __first now equals __last it breaks, otherwise it swaps the elements at __first and __last with _IterOps<_AlgPolicy>::iter_swap and increments __first. It returns void. The elements of the range are reversed in place; the local __first and __last end equal, at the original __first advanced by floor(n/2) for n elements (for n == 0 nothing is done, for n == 1 only __last is decremented). Only iterator equality is used, so no element ordering is required.
note: Round-1/2 reviewers wrong (parity and final positions are as the old prose said: n=1 first unchanged, n=2 first==last==orig+1, n=3 orig+1, n=4 orig+2; reverse.h:29-36); round-15 point (no ordering requirement) is true but this overload's old prose did not claim one.

name: __reverse_impl(_RandomAccessIterator, _RandomAccessIterator, random_access_iterator_tag)
prose: Template function in libc++ (__cxx03/__algorithm/reverse.h) taking its two iterators by value. If __first != __last it runs for (; __first < --__last; ++__first) with iter_swap(__first, __last) in the body, i.e. it swaps symmetric elements until the iterators meet or cross, and returns void. The range is reversed in place. The local iterators end, for n >= 1, as __first == __last == original first advanced by (n-1)/2 when n is odd, and for even n >= 2 as __first = original first advanced by n/2 with __last one position before it; for n == 0 nothing happens. Only iterator comparison (<) is used, not element ordering.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: the old prose required the elements to be ordered by <; the code compares iterators only. Parity claims were already right (reverse.h:40-44).

name: search_n(_ForwardIterator, _ForwardIterator, _Size, const _Tp&, _BinaryPredicate)
prose: Template function in __cxx03/__algorithm/search_n.h (marked nodiscard) with a static_assert that _BinaryPredicate is callable with (*first, const _Tp&). It converts __count with __convert_to_integral and returns the .first of __search_n_impl(first, last, count, value, pred, identity). For forward (non-random-access) iterators the forward implementation returns __first when count <= 0, otherwise the start of the first run of count consecutive elements for which pred(element, value) is true, or __last if none. For random-access iterators the implementation returns __first when count == 0, returns __last when the range is shorter than count, and otherwise scans the same way using a precomputed last start position. A negative count is not handled in the random-access implementation (the test count == 0 is false and the short-range test is not triggered), so it can scan and read beyond the end instead of returning __first.
note: Round-15/17 reviewers right: search_n.h:72-77 only tests count == 0 and size < count; the forward version tests count <= 0 (line 34). Old prose said __first for count <= 0 on all paths.

name: search_n(_ForwardIterator, _ForwardIterator, _Size, const _Tp&)
prose: Template function in __cxx03/__algorithm/search_n.h (marked nodiscard): returns std::search_n(first, last, __convert_to_integral(count), value, __equal_to()), so it behaves as the predicate overload with equality. For forward iterators it returns __first for count <= 0, the start of the first run of count consecutive elements equal to value, or __last if none; for random-access iterators it returns __first only for count == 0 and a negative count is not handled (it can read beyond the end).
note: Round-15/17 reviewers right (see the predicate overload).

name: __set_intersection(_InForwardIter1, _Sent1, _InForwardIter2, _Sent2, _OutIter, _Compare&&, forward_iterator_tag, forward_iterator_tag)
prose: Template function in __cxx03/__algorithm/set_intersection.h returning __set_intersection_result {__in1_, __in2_, __out_}. Forward-iterator overload using one-sided binary search. While __first2 != __last2 it advances __first1 with __lower_bound_onesided to the first element not less than *__first2 and calls __set_intersection_add_output_if_equal, then (unless __first1 reached __last1, which ends the loop) advances __first2 by __lower_bound_onesided against *__first1 and calls the helper again. The helper copies *__first1 to *__result, increments __result, __first1 and __first2 when two consecutive probes both found the iterators possibly equal. The result's __out_ is the output iterator after the last element written, and __in1_ and __in2_ are _IterOps::next(__first1, __last1) and next(__first2, __last2), which for same-typed iterator and sentinel is __last1 and __last2 respectively. The elements of both inputs are only read.
note: All three reviewers wrong: the returned input iterators are __last1 and __last2 (iterator_operations.h:112-114 next(_Iterator, _Iterator __last) returns __last), not one or two past the last examined element; the old prose was also wrong. set_intersection.h:86-119.

name: __set_intersection(_InInputIter1, _Sent1, _InInputIter2, _Sent2, _OutIter, _Compare&&, input_iterator_tag, input_iterator_tag)
prose: Template function in __cxx03/__algorithm/set_intersection.h returning __set_intersection_result {__in1_, __in2_, __out_}. Single-pass overload. While both ranges are non-empty: if comp(*first1, *first2) it advances first1; otherwise, if also !comp(*first2, *first1) it copies *first1 to *result, increments result and first1, and then advances first2 in either case of the else branch. The result holds __out_ = the output iterator after the last write and __in1_ = _IterOps::next(first1, last1) and __in2_ = next(first2, last2), which for same-typed iterator and sentinel equal __last1 and __last2. The inputs are only read.
note: Reviewers wrong as above (set_intersection.h:130-156).

name: __set_intersection(_InIter1, _Sent1, _InIter2, _Sent2, _OutIter, _Compare&&) [dispatcher]
prose: Template function in __cxx03/__algorithm/set_intersection.h returning __set_intersection_result {__in1_, __in2_, __out_}. Dispatcher: forwards the arguments to the six-argument-plus-tags __set_intersection, passing the iterator category tags of the two iterator types from _IterOps<_AlgPolicy>::__iterator_category; when both categories derive from forward_iterator_tag the forward (binary search) overload is selected, otherwise the input-iterator overload, and the selected overload's result is returned unchanged.
note: Reviewers wrong: __in1_ and __in2_ come from the chosen overload and equal __last1/__last2 (see overloads). set_intersection.h:158-170.

name: random_shuffle(_RandomAccessIterator, _RandomAccessIterator)
prose: Template function in __cxx03/__algorithm/shuffle.h (C++03 random_shuffle with the default random source). It computes d = last - first and does nothing if d <= 1. Otherwise it creates a uniform_int_distribution<ptrdiff_t> and takes __g = __rs_get() (the library's default random source). It decrements __last and d, so d starts at n-1 for n elements, and loops while __first < __last: i = distribution(g, range [0, d]) (inclusive, d = the number of elements after *__first); if i != 0 it swaps *__first with *(__first + i); then ++__first and --d. The iterators are the function's own copies. So the element at each position (except the last) is swapped with a uniformly chosen element at or after it. Returns void; no iterators are invalidated.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: the distribution bound is d = (n-1-k) at step k, i.e. the old prose's 'd = last - first' was one too large (shuffle.h:98-106). Reviewers of rounds 1 and 2 concerned the three-argument overload.

name: random_shuffle(_RandomAccessIterator, _RandomAccessIterator, _RandomNumberGenerator&&)
prose: Template function in __cxx03/__algorithm/shuffle.h taking a caller-supplied generator __rand. It computes d = last - first (n elements) and does nothing if d <= 1. Otherwise it decrements __last and loops while __first < __last: i = __rand(d), swapping *__first with *(__first + i) if i != 0, then ++__first and --d. So __rand is called with d = n, n-1, ..., 2 (n-1 calls) and the result must be in [0, d) for the swap to stay inside the range (not checked). Returns void; elements are permuted by swaps.
note: Reviewers (rounds 1, 2, 15) wrong: the code calls __rand(n) first and stops at __rand(2) (shuffle.h:114-121), which is what the old prose said.

name: __libcpp_clz(unsigned __x)
prose: Inline noexcept function in __cxx03/__bit/countl.h: the overload for unsigned int returns __builtin_clz(__x), the number of leading zero bits in __x within the width of unsigned int; the result is undefined when __x == 0. The file has sibling overloads with the same name returning __builtin_clzl for unsigned long, __builtin_clzll for unsigned long long, and (when 128-bit integers are available) a combination of the clz of the two 64-bit halves or __builtin_clzg, giving results up to 63 or 127.
note: Contract cleared: it fit only the unsigned overload (reviewer round 15 right); the formal's shift is fine for result in 0..31 (rounds 1, 2 wrong). countl.h:29-57.

name: __safe_nanosecond_cast(chrono::duration<_Rep, _Period>) [floating-point _Rep]
prose: Inline template function (enabled when _Rep is floating point) returning chrono::nanoseconds: computes __result_float = __d.count() * num / den of ratio_divide<_Period, nano> in _Rep; returns nanoseconds::max() if that is >= numeric_limits<nanoseconds::rep>::max() (compared in _Rep), nanoseconds::min() if it is <= the minimum, and otherwise nanoseconds(static_cast<rep>(result)), truncating toward zero. A NaN input skips both tests and reaches the cast, whose result is undefined.
note: checked against __cxx03/__condition_variable/condition_variable.h:96-114

name: __safe_nanosecond_cast(chrono::duration<_Rep, _Period>) [non-floating _Rep]
prose: Inline template function (enabled when _Rep is not floating point) returning chrono::nanoseconds: returns nanoseconds(0) if __d.count() == 0; nanoseconds::max() if count > 0 and count > max/num of ratio_divide<_Period, nano>; nanoseconds::min() if count < 0 and count < min/num; otherwise nanoseconds(count * num / den) computed in nanoseconds::rep with integer division, except that a result of 0 (a nonzero duration shorter than 1 ns after truncation, positive or negative) is replaced by nanoseconds(1).
note: lines 116-141

name: condition_variable::wait(unique_lock<mutex>&, _Predicate)
prose: Member function template: while (!__pred()) it calls wait(__lk), the non-predicate wait declared _NOEXCEPT in this header, and then returns void. If __pred() is true on entry it returns without touching __lk. The condition for the predicate evaluation to be under the lock (that __lk owns its mutex) is the caller's precondition; the called wait is noexcept, so a failure inside it ends in termination rather than a thrown system_error. An exception from __pred() propagates.
note: Old prose said system_error is thrown; wait(unique_lock&) is declared _NOEXCEPT (line 60, defined as 'throw()' in C++03 mode), so errors cannot propagate. condition_variable.h:144-148.

name: condition_variable::wait_until(unique_lock<mutex>&, const time_point<_Clock, _Duration>&, _Predicate)
prose: Member function template: while (!__pred()) it calls the time-point wait_until(__lk, __t); if that returns cv_status::timeout it returns the value of one more __pred() call (possibly true), otherwise it loops again; when __pred() becomes true it returns true. If __pred() is true on entry it returns true without waiting. The time-point wait_until returns timeout without waiting when __t <= _Clock::now() and otherwise calls __do_timed_wait, which is _NOEXCEPT: if __lk does not own its mutex or the pthread wait fails other than by timeout, the system_error raised there ends in termination instead of reaching the caller. Exceptions from __pred() propagate.
note: Old prose said system_error is thrown to the caller; __do_timed_wait is _NOEXCEPT (declared at lines 84-92). condition_variable.h:165-173.

name: condition_variable::wait_for(unique_lock<mutex>&, const duration<_Rep, _Period>&, _Predicate)
prose: Member function template: returns wait_until(__lk, chrono::steady_clock::now() + __d, std::move(__pred)). The returned bool is true if the predicate became true (also true if it became true only after the deadline was observed, since one final __pred() is evaluated after a timeout), and false if the predicate is false after the deadline. If __pred() is true on entry it returns true without waiting. Errors raised in the noexcept __do_timed_wait (lock not owned, or pthread wait failure other than timeout) end in termination, not in an exception reaching the caller.
note: Old prose: 'throws system_error' wrong, see above. condition_variable.h:202-206.

name: condition_variable::__do_timed_wait(unique_lock<mutex>&, time_point<steady_clock, nanoseconds>) [clockwait]
prose: Private member, defined only when _LIBCPP_HAS_COND_CLOCKWAIT and declared _NOEXCEPT. If __lk does not own its mutex it calls __throw_system_error(EPERM, ...); because the function is noexcept (throw() in this C++03 configuration) this ends in termination rather than an exception reaching the caller. Otherwise it converts the nanoseconds since epoch to a timespec (seconds via duration_cast; if the seconds count is not below the maximum tv_sec it uses tv_sec = max and tv_nsec = 999999999) and calls pthread_cond_clockwait(&__cv_, mutex native handle, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &ts); ETIMEDOUT is a normal outcome, and any other nonzero result calls __throw_system_error (again terminating). On a normal return the mutex is held again.
note: Old prose said system_error is thrown; the function is _NOEXCEPT. lines 208-229.

name: condition_variable::__do_timed_wait(unique_lock<mutex>&, time_point<_Clock, nanoseconds>) [generic clock template]
prose: Private member template declared _NOEXCEPT: it evaluates __tp - _Clock::now() and calls wait_for(__lk, thatDuration), ignoring the returned cv_status. wait_for returns immediately, without checking __lk, if the duration is not positive; otherwise the wait goes through wait_for's timed wait with the other __do_timed_wait overloads. Because this function is noexcept, an exception arising from the nested calls (lock not owned, wait failure) ends in termination instead of propagating. It returns nothing.
note: Old prose said errors are propagated to the caller; wrong because of _NOEXCEPT. lines 232-236.

name: __libcpp_locale_guard::~__libcpp_locale_guard() [MSVCRT variant]
prose: Destructor of the _LIBCPP_MSVCRT_LIKE variant of __libcpp_locale_guard. If __locale_all is non-null (the constructor changed the locale and saved the old LC_ALL string with _strdup) it calls __setlocale(__locale_all), which calls setlocale(LC_ALL, ...) and throws bad_alloc (via __throw_bad_alloc) if setlocale returns null; if that happens, the free of __locale_all and the _configthreadlocale(__status) call below are skipped. Otherwise it frees __locale_all. Then, when reached, it calls _configthreadlocale(__status) to restore the previous per-thread locale mode. If __locale_all is null it only restores the thread-locale mode. It returns nothing.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: 'in all cases' was wrong because the setlocale failure path throws before free/_configthreadlocale (locale_guard.h:54-64, 65-70).

name: unique_lock::operator=(unique_lock&&)
prose: noexcept move assignment: if this lock owns its mutex (__owns_) it calls __m_->unlock(); then it copies __u's mutex pointer and ownership flag into this object, sets __u's pointer to nullptr and its flag to false, and returns *this. For a self-move-assignment (this == &__u) the owned mutex is unlocked first and the final assignments leave this object with a null mutex pointer and no ownership, so the lock is released and the association is lost.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: the old prose claimed self-assignment keeps __u's state (unique_lock.h:78-87).

name: operator<<(basic_ostream&, const cauchy_distribution<_RT>&)
prose: Stream insertion operator template (__cxx03/__random/cauchy_distribution.h). It creates a __save_flags guard on __os, which records the stream's flags and fill character and restores both when the function returns. It then sets the flags to dec | left | fixed | scientific, sets the fill to the widened space, writes __x.a(), the space character and __x.b() with the stream's own insertion operators (any stream failure is handled by those operators, not by this function), and returns __os.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: __save_flags restores the fill as well (iosfwd:144-162); the old prose said the fill is not restored.

name: mersenne_twister_engine::__seed(_Sseq&, integral_constant<unsigned, 1>)
prose: Private member template of mersenne_twister_engine seeding the state from a seed sequence __q. It generates __n 32-bit words into a local array with __q.generate(__ar, __ar + __n) and sets each __x_[i] = static_cast<result_type>(__ar[i] & _Max) (for i in 0..__n-1). __mask is all ones if __r equals the digit count of result_type, otherwise (1 << __r) - 1. It then sets __i_ = 0. If (__x_[0] & ~__mask) == 0, it scans the remaining words and returns early (leaving __x_[0] as assigned) as soon as any __x_[i] (i >= 1) is nonzero; if all of them are zero it sets __x_[0] = result_type(1) << (__w - 1). Otherwise (some bit of __x_[0] above the mask is set) it leaves the state as assigned. It returns nothing.
note: Original reviewer wrong about the mask, round-15 reviewer right that the early return is taken when a later word is nonzero, not after the overwrite (mersenne_twister_engine.h:587-602).

name: mersenne_twister_engine::__seed(_Sseq&, integral_constant<unsigned, 2>)
prose: Private member template of mersenne_twister_engine seeding the state from a seed sequence __q. It generates 2*__n 32-bit words into a local array with __q.generate and sets each __x_[i] = static_cast<result_type>((__ar[2*i] + ((uint64_t)__ar[2*i+1] << 32)) & _Max). __mask is all ones if __r equals the digit count of result_type, otherwise (1 << __r) - 1. It then sets __i_ = 0. If (__x_[0] & ~__mask) == 0, it scans the remaining words and returns early (leaving __x_[0] as assigned) as soon as any __x_[i] (i >= 1) is nonzero; if all of them are zero it sets __x_[0] = result_type(1) << (__w - 1). Otherwise (some bit of __x_[0] above the mask is set) it leaves the state as assigned. It returns nothing.
note: as above (mersenne_twister_engine.h:619-634)

name: expected::operator=(expected&&)
prose: Member of std::expected in <__expected/expected.h>. Constrained to move-constructible and move-assignable _Tp and _Err with at least one of them nothrow move constructible; noexcept when both moves are nothrow. If both objects hold values it move-assigns the value; if both hold errors it move-assigns the error (no strong guarantee for these two same-state cases). If the states differ it calls __reinit_expected, which destroys the held alternative and constructs the new one from the moved source: directly if construction is nothrow, via a temporary if the new type is nothrow move constructible, otherwise it saves the old value in a temporary and restores it if construction throws. It returns *this; __rhs is left valid but unspecified.
note: Round-15 reviewer's point concerns the rvalue unexpected assignment, not this function; the old prose was correct here. expected.h:652-669 and 607-627.

name: expected::operator=(_Up&&)
prose: Member of std::expected in <__expected/expected.h>. Template taking a value convertible to _Tp; constrained so that _Up is not expected or unexpected, _Tp is constructible and assignable from _Up and at least one of nothrow constructing _Tp from _Up, nothrow move constructing _Tp, or nothrow move constructing _Err holds. If *this holds a value it assigns __v to it (no strong guarantee if that throws); otherwise it calls __reinit_expected to destroy the error and construct a value from __v, restoring the previous error if construction throws (via a temporary of the old state when needed). It returns *this.
note: Round-15 reviewer's point concerns the rvalue unexpected assignment, not this function. expected.h:671-684.

name: expected::operator=(const unexpected<_OtherErr>&)
prose: Member of std::expected in <__expected/expected.h>. Constrained by __can_assign_from_unexpected<const _OtherErr&>: _Err constructible and assignable from const _OtherErr&, and at least one of nothrow constructing _Err, nothrow move constructing _Tp or _Err. If *this holds a value it calls __reinit_expected to destroy the value and construct an error from __un.error() (restoring the previous value if construction throws); if it holds an error it assigns __un.error() to it (no strong guarantee if that throws). It returns *this. The separate rvalue overload taking unexpected<_OtherErr>&& moves the error instead.
note: Round-15 reviewer's remark is about that other (rvalue) overload; this const& overload matches the old prose. expected.h:697-706.

name: __estimated_width
prose: Constexpr noexcept function in __format/width_estimation_table.h (the slice cut the head; the real name is __estimated_width, taking const char32_t __code_point) returning int. It returns 1 if __code_point is above __table_upper_bound, or below the start of the first table entry (__entries[0] >> 14). Otherwise it finds, with ranges::upper_bound on __entries using the key (__code_point << 14) | 0x3fff, the first entry whose start is greater than the code point; if that is index 0 it returns 1. Else it takes the previous entry, whose upper bound is its start (entry >> 14) plus its low 14 bits (entry & 0x3fff), and returns 2 if __code_point <= that upper bound (inclusive), otherwise 1. Each table entry packs a range start in the high bits and the offset to the range's last code point in the low 14 bits. It has no side effects.
note: Old name __estimate_width does not exist; entries encode start << 14 | offset to range end (width_estimation_table.h:244-265). Table must be sorted.

name: __bind_r::operator()(_Args&&...) const
prose: Const-qualified call operator of __bind_r in __functional/bind.h, enabled when the result of __bind_return<const _Fd, const _Td, tuple<_Args&&...>> is convertible to result_type (_Rp) or _Rp is void. It returns std::__invoke_r<_Rp>(static_cast<base const&>(*this), std::forward<_Args>(__args)...): the stored callable and bound arguments are used through const references, the call is made with the supplied arguments, the result is converted to _Rp (nothing returned if _Rp is void), and exceptions from the call propagate. A separate non-const operator() overload (bind.h:253-260) does the same through a non-const reference. No state of the bind object is modified by the const overload itself.
note: Round-15 reviewer's point (the non-const overload exists) is true but is a different function.

name: __policy_func<_Rp(_ArgTypes...)>::operator()(_ArgTypes&&...) const
prose: Const call operator of the type-erased __policy_func in __functional/function.h: it returns __func_(std::addressof(__buf_), std::forward<_ArgTypes>(__args)...), i.e. the result of calling the stored erased function pointer with the address of the storage buffer and the forwarded arguments. A default-constructed object has __func_ = __empty_func, which calls std::__throw_bad_function_call() (no value returned). After operator=(nullptr) __func_ is set to a null pointer, and after the move constructor or move assignment moves from a source whose policy has a destroy function, the source's __func_ is also set to null; calling through a null __func_ is undefined behavior, not a bad_function_call. In the converting constructor for a null callable __func_ is not initialized by that constructor.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: nullptr assignment sets __func_ to {} (function.h:498-505), only the default constructor uses __empty_func (line 454).

name: operator()(auto __a, auto __b) [lambda __magnitude_geq in ranges::__advance_fn::operator()]
prose: Generic lambda local to ranges::advance's bounded overload (__iterator/advance.h:157): returns __a == 0 ? __b == 0 : __a > 0 ? __a >= __b : __a <= __b. When __a and __b have the same sign (or zero), it is true exactly when |__a| >= |__b|; for operands of different signs the formula does not compute a magnitude comparison. It has no side effects.
note: Previously dropped; the lambda call operator is a function, fixed from the source line.

name: operator-(const move_sentinel<_Sent>& __x, const move_iterator& __y)
prose: Hidden friend of move_iterator, constrained to sized_sentinel_for<_Sent, _Iter> (C++20): returns __x.base() - __y.base() as iter_difference_t<_Iter>, i.e. the sentinel position minus the iterator position (the number of increments from the wrapped iterator to the wrapped sentinel when that is nonnegative). It has no other effects. The other friend overload operator-(const move_iterator&, const move_sentinel<_Sent>&) returns __x.base() - __y.base() with the operands the other way round.
note: Round-15 reviewer wrong as stated: sentinel minus iterator is the distance from the iterator to the sentinel; the old prose said that. move_iterator.h:220-224.

name: num_get::do_get(iter_type, iter_type, ios_base&, ios_base::iostate&, bool&) const
prose: Member function reading a bool. If ios_base::boolalpha is not set in __iob.flags(): it sets __lv = -1, calls the long overload of do_get (which normally stores the parsed value, or 0 after setting failbit when parsing fails, into __lv), then sets __v = false if __lv == 0, __v = true if __lv == 1, and for any other value sets __v = true and assigns __err = ios_base::failbit exactly (overwriting any other bits such as eofbit). If boolalpha is set it gets the ctype and numpunct facets of the stream's locale, builds the two names truename() and falsename(), calls __scan_keyword (which consumes matching characters, sets failbit in __err if neither name matches and eofbit if the input ends), and sets __v = true exactly when the first name (truename) was matched, false otherwise. It returns the input iterator after the characters consumed.
note: Old prose said a failed parse leaves the long at -1 and gives true; the standard long overload stores 0 on failure (__num_get_signed_integral returns 0 and sets failbit, num.h:277-299), so __v becomes false there and the failbit comes from the long parse. num.h:624-650.

name: num_get::do_get(iter_type, iter_type, ios_base&, ios_base::iostate&, void*&) const
prose: Member function reading a pointer value. It reads characters while __stage2_int_loop (base 16, empty grouping string, null thousands separator) accepts them, growing an internal string buffer as needed, and stops at the first rejected character or at __e. It then calls sscanf with "%p" on the collected text storing into __v; if that does not return 1 it assigns __err = ios_base::failbit (replacing any earlier bits) and leaves __v unchanged; otherwise __err keeps its incoming bits and __v holds the parsed pointer. Finally, if the loop ended because __b == __e it ORs eofbit into __err. It returns the iterator after the consumed characters.
note: Old prose correct; checked against num.h:653-689.

name: layout_right::mapping::operator()(_Indices... __idx) const noexcept
prose: Member of layout_right::mapping (C++23), enabled when the number of indices equals the rank and each is convertible to index_type and nothrow constructible. It first evaluates _LIBCPP_ASSERT_UNCATEGORIZED(__is_multidimensional_index_in(__extents_, __idx...), "out of bounds indexing"): the check is made only in assertion-enabled builds (the source comment says it is intentionally not a hardened-mode check) and a failing check is diagnosed through the assertion handler, otherwise it is unchecked. It then returns, computed in index_type with a fold over the ranks, __res = idx_r + extent(r) * __res from the first to the last index, which equals the row-major linear offset sum of idx_r times the product of the later extents; for in-bounds indices the result is below required_span_size(). It does not modify the mapping.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: the assertion is _LIBCPP_ASSERT_UNCATEGORIZED, not a hardened assertion (layout_right.h:149-161).

name: unique_ptr::unique_ptr()
prose: Constructor template (constexpr noexcept) enabled only when the deleter type is default constructible and not a pointer type (_EnableIfDeleterDefaultConstructible). It value-initializes the stored pointer (null) and value-initializes the stored deleter. Nothing else is done and it cannot throw.
note: Round-1 and round-15 reviewers wrote about the converting/move constructors; for the zero-argument, nullptr_t, pointer and deleter constructors their point does not apply. unique_ptr.h:185-221.

name: unique_ptr::unique_ptr(nullptr_t)
prose: Constructor template (constexpr noexcept) enabled under the same condition as the default constructor (deleter default constructible and not a pointer type). It ignores its argument, value-initializes the stored pointer (null) and the deleter.
note: Round-1 and round-15 reviewers wrote about the converting/move constructors; for the zero-argument, nullptr_t, pointer and deleter constructors their point does not apply. unique_ptr.h:185-221.

name: unique_ptr::unique_ptr(pointer)
prose: Explicit constructor template (noexcept) enabled only when the deleter is default constructible and not a pointer type. It stores __p as the managed pointer and value-initializes the deleter. The unique_ptr then owns __p (if non-null) and its deleter will be applied to it; the caller must not delete __p itself.
note: Round-1 and round-15 reviewers wrote about the converting/move constructors; for the zero-argument, nullptr_t, pointer and deleter constructors their point does not apply. unique_ptr.h:185-221.

name: unique_ptr::unique_ptr(pointer, _LValRefType<_Dummy>)
prose: Constructor template (noexcept) enabled only when the deleter is constructible from the parameter type, which is const _Dp& for a non-reference deleter, _Dp& for an lvalue-reference deleter and const _Dp& for a const-reference deleter. It stores __p and direct-initializes the stored deleter from __d: a copy for a non-reference deleter (the caller's __d is unchanged) or a reference bound to __d for a reference deleter (so __d must outlive the unique_ptr). The unique_ptr owns __p if non-null.
note: Round-1 and round-15 reviewers wrote about the converting/move constructors; for the zero-argument, nullptr_t, pointer and deleter constructors their point does not apply. unique_ptr.h:185-221.

name: unique_ptr::unique_ptr(pointer, _GoodRValRefType<_Dummy>)
prose: Constructor template (noexcept) enabled only for a non-reference deleter type constructible from _Dp&&. It stores __p and constructs the deleter from std::move(__d): a move construction if _Dp has one (leaving __d moved-from), otherwise a copy (leaving __d as it was); a static_assert rejects a reference deleter type. The unique_ptr owns __p if non-null. A separate deleted overload covers the bad rvalue-reference deleter cases.
note: Round-1 and round-15 reviewers wrote about the converting/move constructors; for the zero-argument, nullptr_t, pointer and deleter constructors their point does not apply. unique_ptr.h:185-221.

name: unique_ptr::unique_ptr(unique_ptr&&)
prose: Move constructor (noexcept): stores __u.release() (so __u is left with a null pointer and this object owns the resource) and constructs the deleter from std::forward<deleter_type>(__u.get_deleter()): for a non-reference deleter that is an rvalue, so it uses the deleter's move constructor if it has one (leaving __u's deleter moved-from) and otherwise copies it (leaving it unchanged); for an lvalue-reference deleter the new deleter refers to the same object as __u's.
note: Round-15 reviewer right: a non-reference deleter may be copied rather than moved. unique_ptr.h:211-213.

name: unique_ptr::unique_ptr(unique_ptr<_Up, _Ep>&&)
prose: Converting move constructor template (noexcept), enabled when _Up is not an array type, _Up's pointer type converts to this pointer type, and the deleter is convertible: for a reference _Dp, _Ep must be the same type as _Dp; for a non-reference _Dp, _Ep must be convertible to _Dp. It stores __u.release() (leaving __u null) and constructs the deleter from std::forward<_Ep>(__u.get_deleter()): for a non-reference _Ep that is an rvalue (moved from if a converting move exists, otherwise copied), for an lvalue-reference _Ep the deleter is copied or a reference is bound to the same object (as the case requires).
note: Round-1 reviewer's 'same type' point was already in the prose; round-15 reviewer right that a non-reference deleter may be copied, not necessarily moved. unique_ptr.h:215-221.
